title: The Washington Agreement: Ending the War Within the War
sources: ICTY Prlic et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T)
content:
By the winter of 1993-94, the war between Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats had devastated central Bosnia and Herzegovina for nearly a year. What had begun as localized clashes over territorial control in the Lašva Valley and Mostar had escalated into a full-scale conflict, complete with concentration camps, forced expulsions, and the systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure. The siege of East Mostar by HVO forces, the massacres at Ahmići and Stupni Do, and the internment of Bosniak civilians in camps such as Dretelj and Gabela had generated international revulsion. Meanwhile, the VRS continued to press its advantages across eastern Bosnia and around Sarajevo, exploiting the Bosniak-Croat division to consolidate territorial gains. The war within the war was destroying both peoples while serving only their common enemy.

The diplomatic intervention that ended the Bosniak-Croat conflict was driven primarily by the United States. American envoys, working through a series of negotiations in late 1993 and early 1994, brokered discussions between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, with Bosnian Croat political leaders brought into the process through Zagreb's influence. President Franjo Tuđman's willingness to pressure Bosnian Croat leaders proved decisive. Croatia's own strategic calculations played a role — international isolation over HVO conduct in Bosnia was damaging Zagreb's broader ambitions, including eventual European integration and the recovery of Serb-held Krajina.

The Washington Agreement, signed on 18 March 1994, ended hostilities between Bosniak and Bosnian Croat forces and established the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a joint political entity. The Federation would comprise Bosniak-majority and Croat-majority cantons, with shared governance structures at the federal level. A preliminary agreement on a confederation between the Federation and the Republic of Croatia was also outlined, though this element remained largely aspirational. The agreement did not resolve the underlying territorial disputes — particularly the status of Mostar and central Bosnian towns — but it imposed a ceasefire framework that broadly held.

The military consequences were immediate and profound. HVO and ARBiH forces, which had been engaged across a complex and fragmented front in central Bosnia, Herzegovina, and the Neretva valley, ceased offensive operations against one another. Brigades that had been committed to the Bosniak-Croat front became available for redeployment against the VRS. For the ARBiH, this was transformative — formations that had been fighting on two fronts simultaneously could now concentrate their strength. For the HVO, the agreement provided relief from a conflict they were increasingly losing in central Bosnia, where ARBiH offensives in late 1993 had made significant gains.

The ICTY Prlić et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T) examined the Bosniak-Croat conflict in extensive detail, establishing that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and its military arm, the HVO, had pursued a systematic campaign against the Bosniak population in areas claimed for a Croat entity. The Washington Agreement effectively ended this campaign, though accountability for the crimes committed during it would take years to establish through international judicial proceedings.

For the Bosnian Serb leadership in Pale, the Washington Agreement represented a strategic setback of the first order. The Bosniak-Croat war had been an enormous advantage — dividing their opponents and allowing the VRS to operate against weakened, distracted adversaries. A unified Federation, backed by American diplomatic engagement and the prospect of military cooperation between former enemies, fundamentally altered the balance of the conflict heading into its final phase.
